outputs.L1:
**Polished Version**

Somewhere in Kentucky, she went for kicks—
spiked polka-dot mint julep, Grade 1 Stakes,
white-gloved clubhouse how-do-you-do's—
until all the horses broke their legs.

And for all the horses, my ex
joined the Seine-et-Oise Thoroughbred Liberation Front
and crashed all the Bentleys,
yet it was I who bled
in Derby countryside,
where horses die in Japanese slaughterhouses,
defrocked of rose blanket and blue ribbon.

And how completely they departed
into the kind of darkness
that knows only my old Kentucky home—
no longer a run for the roses,
now besieged with cannibals and thieves,
where only Millionaires' Row still sings:

*A hero is a horse without a heart
that never aches for the lovers who cross them
one too many times.
When we kill one horse, all of them die,
waiting—long after Kentucky.*

And she slips white gloves onto my hands,
bent from carrying her through NYC streets
jammed the wrong way in every direction.
How merry are we—how merry,
how bright-shine beaming, no longer weeping.

And she bears my head to the heat,
and I let it all go,
and bet my last hat and home.
And how—how completely are we—
and it changes everything.

---

outputs.L2: Somewhere in Kentucky she chased her thrills—dressed in polka-dot heels and mint julep, a Grade 1 stakes race, that white-gloved clubhouse greeting—right up until every horse shattered its legs. And on behalf of all those horses, my former lover took up with the Seine-et-Oise Thoroughbred Liberation Front and smashed every Bentley, though it was me who ended up bleeding out in Derby country, where horses meet their end in Japanese slaughterhouses, stripped of their rose garlands and blue ribbons—and oh, how gracefully they departed, into a darkness that recognized nothing but my old Kentucky home, which is no longer a run for the roses but rather overrun by cannibals and thieves, where only Millionaires Row still sings that a hero is simply a horse with no heart, one that never aches for the lovers who betray it far too often—because when a single horse dies, they all perish, still waiting long after Kentucky, and she pulls white gloves over my hands, twisted from hauling her through New York City streets that snarl the wrong way in every direction. How joyful are we, how joyful, how radiantly glowing and no longer in tears—and she carries my head toward the warmth, and I surrender completely, wagering my final hat and my home, and how, oh how joyful are we, and it transforms everything.
outputs.L3:
# The Old Kentucky Home

There was a woman in Kentucky I remember still—one who lived entirely inside the glamour of it all. She wore the culture of Grand Prix horse racing like a second skin: the mint juleps sweating in silver cups, the pristine white gloves, the elaborate rituals of the clubhouse that separated those who belonged from those who merely watched. To her, this was a world of refinement, of upper-class ease, of afternoons that seemed to promise they would never end.

But the beauty of that world was only ever a surface. Beneath it lay something crueler. The horses—those magnificent animals bred for speed and spectacle—would break their legs on the track and die. In those moments the brutality of the sport revealed itself, stripped of its finery, no different in the end from the Japanese slaughterhouses where such creatures meet their industrial fate. The glory and the killing, it turned out, were two faces of the same thing.

She could not bear it. My ex-partner turned against the whole machinery of the racing world and joined the Seine-et-Oise Thoroughbred Liberation Front, throwing herself into acts of rebellion. She crashed Bentleys—those gleaming symbols of the very wealth that fueled the sport—smashing them in a fury of protest, as if destruction were the only honest response to a world so thoroughly rotten.

And so I mourn what has become of the beloved old Kentucky home. It has been corrupted, overrun, besieged by cannibals and thieves who feed on what once was pure. Only the wealthy elite remain to celebrate now, raising their glasses amid the ruin, blind or indifferent to the wreckage all around them.

In the end, I surrendered everything. I bet my last hat and my last home, gambling away whatever I had left. Yet it was in a single intimate moment with her—close, quiet, unguarded—that everything shifted. In that instant my entire perspective was transformed, and I understood at last what all of it had truly been worth.
outputs.L4:
# The Weight of a Single Death

The poem opens beneath the wide brim of a Derby hat, all pastels and mint juleps, where spectators gather to witness what they believe is sport. Here, the language fragments deliberately—snatches of a bugle's call, the flash of silk racing colors, the roar of a crowd—each image polished to a bright, deceptive shine. This is the surface the world chooses to see: the pageantry of the Kentucky Derby, an event dressed in tradition and elegance, where beauty conceals what moves beneath it.

But the poem refuses to let that surface hold. Between the celebratory images, it inserts what the glamour is built to obscure: the labored breathing of a horse pushed past its limit, the fragile architecture of legs never meant to bear such punishing speed, the quiet ledger of animals discarded once they can no longer run. The juxtaposition is intentional and unrelenting. For every mention of roses draped across a winner's withers, there is the shadow of the slaughterhouse waiting for the ones who lose, who break, who simply grow old. The poem asks us to hold both realities at once—to see that the spectacle and the suffering are not separate things but two faces of the same enterprise.

At the center of the work is its unifying claim, returned to like a refrain: *when we kill one horse all of them die.* This line functions as the poem's moral engine. It resists the comfortable logic that treats each animal as an isolated case, a single misfortune easily forgotten. Instead, it insists on connection—that cruelty inflicted on one is cruelty made possible for all, that a single death implicates an entire system and everyone who sustains it. The individual horse becomes a stand-in for the many, and the many become inseparable from the one.

This is where the poem turns its gaze toward us. Complicity is its quiet accusation. We are the crowd in our fine clothes, the eyes that admire the race and look away from its cost, the beneficiaries of an entertainment that demands a body in payment. The poem does not shout this charge so much as reveal it, laying the evidence beside the beauty until we cannot separate our pleasure from the harm that funds it.

Yet the poem does not end in despair. Its final movement is one of awakening. To recognize the shared cruelty—to truly understand that one death is every death—is itself a kind of transformation. The poem closes on the conviction that this recognition *changes everything*: that once we see clearly, we cannot unsee, and that the act of seeing carries with it an obligation. What began as pageantry ends as reckoning, and the reader is left holding the knowledge that awareness, however painful, is the first and necessary condition of change.
outputs.L5:
# Somewhere

Somewhere, the sun is rising while it sets for you. Somewhere, a stranger is laughing at a joke you'll never hear, and a child is taking their very first step. The word itself is a quiet promise—a gesture toward a place we cannot see but somehow believe in.

"Somewhere" lives in the space between certainty and hope. When we say we'll find happiness *somewhere*, or that our missing keys must be *somewhere*, we admit we don't yet know the location, but we trust that it exists. It is a word built for dreamers and for the lost, for those searching and those simply wondering what lies beyond the horizon.

There is comfort in the vagueness. Not everything needs a precise address. Some feelings, some memories, some futures are better left as *somewhere*—open, unfinished, full of possibility. The unnamed place can be anywhere we need it to be.

Perhaps that's why the word appears so often in songs and stories. "Somewhere over the rainbow." "Somewhere, someday." It carries longing without demanding answers. It points forward without pretending to know the way.

And so we keep moving, keep hoping, keep believing that somewhere out there is exactly what we've been looking for—waiting patiently for the day we finally arrive.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about the Kentucky Derby, animal rights, and a doomed love affair, using fragmented syntax and no clear line breaks.
counterfactuals.output:
**RUN FOR THE ROSES**

The horses do not know they are famous. Two minutes, the mint dissolving, and somewhere a woman I loved is wearing a hat wide as an argument—we came here to watch the beautiful thing die a little, all of us, hooves like applause against packed dirt, against the eventuality of the glue factory, the syringe, the hushed vet tent behind the grandstand where nobody films—*look at me*, she said, but I was looking at the animal, the froth, the whip that is called a *crop* to make it kinder, the way we rename everything we cannot stop doing—cruelty in a fascinator, love in a losing ticket—I bet on the wrong horse the way I bet on you, blindered, driven, running because the gate opened and running is the only theology a body remembers—thoroughbred: a word meaning *bred through*, meaning *made for this*, meaning *your want engineered into my legs*—she smelled of bourbon and the specific perfume of leaving—the colt named Fortune's Fool went down at the far turn, went down like a sentence I couldn't finish, and they raised the green screen, the mercy tarp, the do-not-look, and the crowd did not stop cheering because the crowd never sees the part after—*you never see the part after*, she said, meaning us, meaning the tarp we'd raise around ourselves—garland of five hundred roses draped over the winner, thorns cut off, of course, everything's thorns cut off, everything made soft enough to swallow—I held her hand and felt the pulse there, that stubborn animal, that thing that runs and runs and does not know it is owned—the odds, the odds, the mud, the beautiful doomed cargo of muscle and my own heart in the sixth race, breaking clean from the gate, already lame, already loved, already—*and they're off*—
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that mixes the glamour of the Kentucky Derby with the darkness of horse slaughter and a broken relationship in New York City.
counterfactuals.output:
**Louisville to Lexington Avenue**

The mint leaves bruise between my fingers
the way your name still bruises when I speak it—
first Saturday in May, and I am wearing
the hat we bought the spring you loved me,
wide brim like a promise, silk the color of a wound.

Here the horses run for roses.
Somewhere else, they run out of luck.

I sip my bourbon on the twentieth floor
of a Manhattan that never smelled of hay,
and think of Dancer's Image, of the ones
who crossed the wire golden and were later
loaded into trailers in the dark,
their racing silks exchanged for auction tags,
the glory rendered down to something
sold by weight.

You left in April.
The odds were never posted for us.
We ran the mile-and-a-quarter of a marriage
and I did not see the far turn coming—
how quickly the crowd forgets a name,
how a body built for beauty
becomes a thing that someone hauls away.

They put the blanket on the winner.
They put the needle in the also-ran.

And I am both, tonight—
the toast and the discarded,
the champagne flute and the kill pen,
the woman in the celebrated hat
who knows that everything they crown
they eventually cash in.

The band plays *My Old Kentucky Home*
and grown men weep into their juleps.
I weep too, but not for Stephen Foster—
I weep for all the running that we did,
for horses I will never save,
for the last good look you gave me
before they led you, led us both,
away from the roses,
into the ordinary dark
where no one keeps the time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde poem about "my old Kentucky home," derbies, Bentleys, white gloves, and betting everything on love.
counterfactuals.output:
# Silks and Long Shots

My old Kentucky home is not a place—
it is a *velocity*,
a bugle splitting the morning
into before and after.

Derby.
Say it like a prayer
you don't believe in.
Say it like the horses say it
with their hooves:
*maybe, maybe, maybe.*

The Bentley idles at the gate,
a black tongue,
chrome-mouthed,
swallowing the mint and the mud
in equal measures of forgetting.

White gloves—
*ah*—
the great lie of clean hands.
We wave them like flags,
like surrenders,
like the ghosts of every wager
that ever kissed the dirt.

Here is the ledger.
Here is my whole heart
laid on the ticket window,
smudged and folded,
bearing your name
in the place where the odds should go.

Twenty to one.
Fifty to one.
*Everything* to one.

And the roses—
they only give roses
to the winners
and the dead.

So run, you fools,
you thundering syllables of chance,
carry my last coin
past the wire,
where love is the only entry
I ever meant to make—

no hedge,
no place,
no show.

Just the mad green fortune
of betting it all
on the animal
that is your beating,
unbroken
*name.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal, densely packed poem where a woman becomes involved in an animal liberation front and the speaker sacrifices everything for her.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Animal Liberation Front Girlfriend

She came to me smelling of ammonia and open cages,
her fingernails still crusted with the mud of mink farms,
a bolt cutter tattooed across her clavicle
like a promise or a warning I chose to misread.

*Everything,* she said, and I heard *everything,*
so I mortgaged my grandmother's teeth,
sold the piano my father died beneath,
gave the deed to our future to a beagle
with electrodes still weeping from its skull.

We drove through nights lit only by liberated fireflies,
her laugh a jimmied lock, her kiss the snap
of a trap releasing something into the dark.
I learned to love the sirens as her music,
learned the constellations of surveillance cameras,
learned to sleep with one eye rendered animal, alert.

She freed the foxes and they took my name.
She freed the rabbits and they took my sleep.
She freed ten thousand chickens from a warehouse
and I stood knee-deep in feathers like the aftermath
of some apocalypse of pillows, some rapture
where only the wingless were left behind—

which was me. Always me, the wingless one,
holding her coat, her manifesto, her bail money,
holding the bag that held the dwindling
of everything I used to call a life.

*Would you die for them?* she asked the mirror,
and the mirror, being honest, showed her me,
already half-transparent, already ghosting
into the noble cause of her attention.

I signed confessions I never authored.
I took the charges like communion wafers.
When they asked me *why,* I said her name
and it sounded like a species going extinct.

Now I am the last of something.
She is somewhere in the Cascades releasing wolves,
and I am here, a cage flung open
onto nothing, onto the terrible freedom
of a man who gave away his final key
and cannot even liberate himself—

though sometimes, in the dark, I paw the door
and howl a little, practicing,
in case she ever comes back
smelling of ammonia and mercy,
to set me loose again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
